title: Praying for the dead
hook: many Christians pray for the dead; others entrust them to God

segments.voice: Yesterday, funerals: two rooms, two moods, one hope underneath. Your line was memory eternal.

Carved at the bottom of an old headstone, under the name and dates, worn soft by rain: R.I.P. It can read like a goodbye. Sleep tight. It's over now. But ask who those letters are talking to. Not the dead person, exactly, and not quite the people walking past. Rest in peace is a request. Somebody is being asked to give that rest. The question under the stone: once someone has died, is there anything left to say to God about them?

First, the words. R.I.P. stands for the Latin requiescat in pace, may he or she rest in peace: a prayer, shortened to fit on stone. Second, those who pray. Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead at funerals, on anniversaries, at Mass or the Divine Liturgy. An old Catholic prayer asks God to give them eternal rest and let perpetual light shine on them. Orthodox services ask God to give rest to the soul of his servant, where there is no pain or sorrow. They point to Second Maccabees, a book in their Bibles, where Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for soldiers who had died, and the book praises praying for the dead. And Paul writes of his friend Onesiphorus: "The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day." Some readers think Onesiphorus had already died; the letter doesn't say. Third, those who entrust. Protestants who follow the Reformers don't pray for the dead. They hold that a person who has died is already safe in God's hands, and nothing needs adding. They can lean on Revelation: "Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours." Rest, already given. So at the grave they give thanks, and let go. Fourth, look at both: one keeps speaking to God about the person, one places the person in God's hands. Both refuse to treat death as the end of God's care. Rest in peace can be either: a prayer, or a hand opening.

Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you still carry, the way they stood or laughed. If you pray for the dead, ask God to give them rest; if you entrust instead, place them in God's hands; if you don't pray, hold them in your thoughts, then open your hands a little. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Praying for the dead. Some Christians keep praying for those who have died; others entrust them to God and give thanks.
Your line: rest in peace. Three letters, and a request inside them. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead at funerals, on anniversaries of a death and in the Mass or Divine Liturgy; in Protestant churches that do not, the dead are commended to God and the service gives thanks for their life.

chat.says: Do Christians pray for people who have already died?
options: Some do, like Catholics and Orthodox; others entrust them to God and give thanks.
No Christians do; once someone has died, there's nothing left to say to God.
All Christians do, at every service, because the Bible plainly commands it.

notes: 'Protestants who follow the Reformers on this don't pray for the dead' stands in for the index hook's 'others'; no proportion is claimed. Some Anglicans and Lutherans do pray for the dead; consider naming that if a Keeper wants more precision.
The Catholic Requiem aeternam and the Orthodox 'give rest, O Lord' prayers are paraphrased, not quoted.
2 Maccabees 12:39–46 paraphrased (Judas sends an offering for fallen soldiers; the book commends praying for the dead). Confirm.
Onesiphorus: whether he had died is debated; the script says the letter does not say. Confirm.
Second Maccabees is called 'a book in their Bibles' (Catholic and Orthodox); the script does not discuss its status in Protestant Bibles.
Original is Latin, not a biblical language; pronunciation given in church Latin.
